slides.title: Generating a Service with Angular CLI 🏗️
slides.content:
# Command Line Magic

Angular CLI can scaffold a service in seconds:

```bash
ng generate service my-service
# shorthand: ng g s my-service
```

This creates two files:
* `my-service.service.ts` – the service class.
* `my-service.service.spec.ts` – the test file.

The service is decorated with `@Injectable()` and registered as a provider in the root injector (by default).

slides.title: The Generated Service

quizData.question: The shorthand command to generate a service is `ng g s ______`.
quizData.explanation: You provide the service name after `ng g s`. E.g., `ng g s user` creates `UserService`.

slides.title: The @Injectable() Decorator 🏷️
slides.content:
`@Injectable()` tells Angular that this class can be injected with dependencies itself (i.e., it can be a dependency).

* If your service has no dependencies, you can technically omit it. But it’s a best practice to always include it.
* The `providedIn: 'root'` option tells Angular to register the service with the root injector, making it available throughout the app as a singleton.

Other possible values for `providedIn`:
* `'root'` – app‑wide singleton.
* `'platform'` – shared across multiple Angular apps on the same page.
* `'any'` – creates a new instance for each lazy‑loaded module.

slides.title: Providing Services in NgModule vs `providedIn`

quizData.question: What does `providedIn: 'root'` do?

options.text: Makes the service available only in the root component.
Registers the service with the root injector, making it a singleton for the whole app.
It prevents the service from being injected anywhere.
It automatically creates an instance for every component.

quizData.explanation: `providedIn: 'root'` provides the service at the application root level, so one instance is shared app‑wide.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Always Use `providedIn: 'root'` Unless You Need a Scoped Service

It keeps configuration minimal and allows tree‑shaking. Only override in specific cases like component‑scoped providers (next lesson).
